common_name: Peach Souffle Daylily (1979 Ida Munson Award Double Peach Daylily)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Registered by hybridizer Lambert, Peach Souffle went on to win the Ida Munson Award in 1979 as the outstanding double-flowered daylily of its year. Plant divisions in average, well-drained garden soil and water regularly through the first season; established dormant clumps are tough and drought-tolerant, needing division only every four to six years. Its clear peach-self double blooms open on sturdy scapes in midseason, holding their full double form more reliably than many early double cultivars.

common_name: Pa Pa Gulino Daylily (1982 Ida Munson Award Pink Blend Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring or early fall with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil.

directions: Registered by Louisiana hybridizer Kenneth G. Durio Jr., Pa Pa Gulino earned the Ida Munson Award in 1982 for its large, silvery flesh-pink blooms with rose-rouge shading above a citron-green throat. The semi-evergreen tetraploid foliage performs best where winters are not severe, and established clumps rebloom readily through the early season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Yazoo Souffle Daylily (1985 Ida Munson Award Fragrant Apricot-Pink Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Yazoo Souffle received the Ida Munson Award in 1985 for its fragrant, light apricot-pink self double blooms on semi-evergreen, diploid plants. It flowers early to midseason and benefits from a sheltered spot in colder parts of its range, where semi-evergreen daylily foliage can suffer dieback. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain bloom count.

common_name: Stroke of Midnight Daylily (1987 Ida Munson Award Bordeaux-Red Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root or potted divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun; evergreen foliage benefits from winter protection in colder zones.

directions: Bred and registered by prolific hybridizer David Kirchhoff, Stroke of Midnight is a fragrant, extra-early-blooming diploid with Bordeaux-red self flowers over a chartreuse throat, winning the Ida Munson Award in 1987 for its striking double form. The evergreen foliage habit means it grows and reblooms over a long season in mild climates but needs mulch protection where winters are harsh. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil and divide every three to four years once clumps become crowded.

common_name: Rachael My Love Daylily (1989 Ida Munson Award Fragrant Golden Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root or potted divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun; evergreen foliage benefits from winter mulch in colder zones.

directions: Registered by hybridizer Talbott, Rachael My Love won the Ida Munson Award in 1989 for its very fragrant, golden-yellow self double blooms on compact, evergreen, diploid plants. It blooms early to midseason and reblooms readily where summers are long. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to keep clumps floriferous.

common_name: Brent Gabriel Daylily (1992 Ida Munson Award Purple Bitone Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root or potted divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun; evergreen foliage benefits from winter protection in colder zones.

directions: Registered by Louisiana hybridizer Lucille S. Guidry, Brent Gabriel received the Ida Munson Award in 1992 for its fragrant purple-bitone double flowers, marked with white watermarks and a green throat. It is an extra-early bloomer with evergreen, diploid foliage and strong rebloom capacity, performing best in warm-winter climates. Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil and divide every three to four years as clumps thicken.

common_name: Ellen Christine Daylily (1994 Ida Munson Award Pink-Gold Blend Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil.

directions: Registered by Louisiana hybridizer Clarence J. Crochet, Ellen Christine won the Ida Munson Award in 1994 for its large, pink-gold blend double blooms over a dark green throat. The semi-evergreen, diploid plant blooms midseason, reblooms through summer, and opens its flowers during daylight hours rather than the evening. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Almost Indecent Daylily (1995 Ida Munson Award Lavender-Cream Double)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil.

directions: Registered by hybridizer Lee Gates, Almost Indecent is a fragrant tetraploid with a lavender-and-cream blend double flower over a chalky chartreuse throat, winning the Ida Munson Award in 1995. Its semi-evergreen foliage blooms early season with an extended bloom habit and good rebloom, performing best where winters are not severe. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years as clumps become crowded.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a compact, non-vining clematis that needs no climbing support.

directions: Andante is a herbaceous, non-climbing selection of the integrifolia group, producing deep mauve-pink, nodding, bell-shaped flowers with light pink margins on twisted tepals from June through September. Unlike true vining clematis it forms an upright, self-supporting clump best used at the front of a sunny border rather than trained on a trellis. Cut the whole plant back close to the ground in late winter, since flowers form only on the current season's growth, and it is a prolific, easy-to-grow choice in cold-winter gardens.

common_name: Twinkle Clematis (Non-Vining White and Sky-Blue Integrifolia)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this compact, non-vining clematis also performs well in containers.

directions: Bred by the Dutch nursery J. van Zoest and sold under the trade name TWINKLE, this integrifolia cultivar (registered name 'Zotwi') bears dainty, scented, bell-shaped flowers that open white with a pale sky-blue crown, fading to pure white in strong sun, from June into September. Its clump-forming, non-clinging stems need no support and work equally well scrambling through low companions or cascading from a container, and the flowers are a favorite of bees. Cut stems back hard in late winter, since bloom occurs only on new growth.

common_name: Hendryetta Clematis (Semi-Nodding Pink Bell Diversifolia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool, in moist but well-drained soil in any aspect from full sun to shade.

directions: A hybrid of the viticella-integrifolia diversifolia group, Hendryetta is a semi-herbaceous, clump-forming scrambler bearing mid-pink, semi-nodding, bell-shaped flowers with prominent deep-pink ribs on the reverse from June through September. Its lax, non-clinging stems do not twine or cling on their own, so weave them through herbaceous perennials, shrubs, or a small obelisk for support. Cut the plant back hard in late winter since it flowers entirely on the current season's growth, and it tolerates a wide range of aspects better than most large-flowered hybrids.

common_name: Prince William Clematis (Tulip-Form Lavender-Mauve Texas Clematis)

planting.note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and roots shaded, training stems up an obelisk or wire trellis in full sun to part shade.

directions: Bred by the Dutch nursery J. van Zoest and registered as 'Zo08171' under the trade name PRINCE WILLIAM, this Texas-clematis hybrid opens purply-red buds into semi-nodding, tulip-shaped flowers with mauve margins over a deep lavender interior, blooming from June into September on new growth. Like its texensis parentage, it tolerates heat and dry spells better than most large-flowered clematis and benefits from roots kept cool and shaded beneath low companion plants. Prune hard in February or March.
